For years, 16830 14th Avenue NW has been more than a residence. It has been the studio of Jan Holbrook Interior Design, the place where an award-winning eye for restraint, light and sightline is practiced every day.

A home like this should not be marketed like the house next door. Buyers in Innis Arden are discerning, design-literate and patient, and the right one will recognize a designer's hand immediately — if we present it with the same discipline Jan brings to her own work. This proposal outlines how we would do exactly that: an editorial story, a technology-forward launch, and a curated First Look befitting one of Shoreline's most protected enclaves.

The Designer

Jan Holbrook,
in her own rooms.

Jan Holbrook's interiors for Gallery House — with DeForest Architects and Joseph McKinstry Construction — took Platinum honors at the Best in American Living Awards and were featured in Luxe Interiors + Design. Her signature: an elegantly minimal backdrop that lets art and view take the lead.

i.

Restraint

Pared, rectilinear forms that never interrupt a sightline. Furnishings chosen for what they leave out as much as what they bring.

ii.

Soft neutrals

Layered linen, stone and sand tones with enough contrast to stay alive — warm walnut against cool glass and steel.

iii.

The view as art

Rooms composed like a gallery, where reflective surfaces carry the outdoors inward and every wall knows what it frames.

Interiors by Jan Holbrook Interior Design. Photography courtesy of the original photographers. Prepared for private presentation.

The Place

Innis Arden,
held in trust.

Platted by The Boeing Company in the 1940s on a wooded bluff above Puget Sound, Innis Arden is a private community of roughly 527 homes, bounded by the Sound, Richmond Beach Road, Boeing Creek and 8th Avenue NW. Protected reserves, private beach access and covenant-guarded views make it one of the rarest addresses north of Seattle — with fewer than a dozen homes trading in a typical year.
